findings.title: The recoverable safety stop becomes an untyped generic CLI failure
findings.trigger: Host enforcement rejects a Packet and the Error leaves the JavaScript call stack through the documented command-line interface.
findings.impact: The next controller cannot select the unavailable-capability repair path from a stable code and may treat it like spawn, auth or malformed-input failure; machine recovery depends on parsing prose.
findings.evidence: HostEnforcementUnavailableError records code UBP_HOST_ENFORCEMENT_UNAVAILABLE and structured admission, but the CLI catch emits only error.message. The compatibility launcher has the same loss at its top-level catch.
findings.suggestion: Project this known error into one bounded JSON failure shape at the existing process boundary and keep unknown exceptions generic; add public-entrypoint tests so code and admission cannot be dropped again.

findings.title: The refusal claims no Host process after process-backed probes may run
findings.trigger: ACP-first driver selection executes identity probes and then the enforcement decision rejects the selected route.
findings.impact: The source contract and resulting recovery narrative assert a stronger no-process boundary than the runtime provides, hiding the only pre-denial execution window from operators and reviewers.
findings.evidence: chooseExecutionDriver is called at line 905 before this block and its production identity inspection spawns commands. The comment at lines 939-940 says no Host process exists, while the error message describes a pre-launch refusal without disclosing those probes.
findings.suggestion: Prevent the probes before denial; if any non-provider preflight remains necessary, name it explicitly in the typed receipt rather than claiming zero Host-side process execution.

positive_observations: The in-process Error preserves redacted dimension statuses and a receipt digest without carrying credential values.
There is no automatic retry or silent fallback after the enforcement decision itself rejects.
